doc.title: Bobby Militello interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 14, 2002

title: Negotiating with agents at Buffalo prices and tracking complaints
summary: He negotiates percentage deals based on Buffalo values, cites Pat Metheny's run, and notes few complaints among 120,000 patrons.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: conditions perfect. And you’re going to love the club. And it’s going to be the right gig, that you’re going to want to come back and play my room again. So we’ll set you up a gross potential based on what we feel is a reasonable market value for that show in Buffalo. Then we’ll put you on a percentage above that if you sell it out completely to the hilt, well then you’ll break in a percentage and we’ll get close to the number you’re looking for. And then the next time you come back we’ll raise the price. Well by doing both ends, and that is negotiating with the agents saying this is Buffalo so let’s go by Buffalo value and prices, let’s not go by New York’s. And that’s what we do and we come up with this mean and we show them — because we don’t lie to them — that when they come in they only drew so many people. And it wasn’t the number he thought he was going to do. And I say well that’s Buffalo. And understand me, the next time maybe we’ll do better. But we’ve broken most of them in the percentage and they walk out with extra money. Especially Pat Methany, he walked out with his full national bread after three days. He was happy as hell, thought it was great. And the Yellow Jackets and all those cats, I mean they do well. So we’ve come up with a formula that’s based on two sides. You look at number one is the club side and the consumer side, and the other side is the agent side and the act side. And you have to balance the two in order to create this thing. And if you look on our web page or whatever, you’ll see that our prices are lower than anybody in the country for these shows. And we all make money. We all make money. Everybody does. The artist leaves happy as hell and everything is cool. And we make a little money in the club on the door. So I don’t expect to make too much money on the door. If I can pay for the act, pay for the stuff and everything else and make a couple of dollars I’d be real happy. It’s more the bar and the food is what we do, and we take a lot of pride in what we do there. The food is very good. It’s short order food but it’s very good. My whole thing is customer service. The customer has to be happy. If he isn’t he has to be able to communicate why he’s not. So there’s always a manager on the floor that everybody will direct their complaint, whether it be a waitress or whatever, to the manager on the floor. The manager will make a decision whether it’s valid or just a hyped complaint just to get the price down or try and get something. If it’s valid we address it and we talk about it in a meeting. They also are free to give out my phone number, not my home number but my office number or my e-mail address, and those people can contact me direct if they think they’re getting sidestepped. And they do contact me direct, and I back, usually, my manager’s decisions because they were right most of the time. But I do communicate with all of those people myself. And they readily — on the bottom of the web page you can click on Bobby M and get to me anyway, everybody can. So the object is we open up the lines of communication so that people can say what they think is wrong. Right now we’re running at around 98 or 99 percent © Fillius Jazz Archive -20-

satisfaction. We only get — we do a little over 120,000 people I think we’re going to do this year, maybe a little more than that. We’re selling out everything lately. And out of that 120,000 people we probably get maybe 20 complaint letters we got this year so far. Maybe 15. And some of them again are the hyped type ones where they just try and get a gift certificate out of it or something like that.
